title: History: change in bowel habit and rectal bleeding in a younger patient

header.contentArea: Communication skills in giving and receiving information and history taking

related.why: The examination that completes this history

brief.scenario: Mrs Helen Marsh, 44, has been referred by her GP on the suspected cancer pathway. She has had six weeks of looser stools with dark blood. Her faecal immunochemical test (FIT) result is 86 µg Hb/g.
brief.task: Take a focused history. You will be stopped at 6 minutes to summarise your history, then asked about investigation and management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Colorectal cancer and colitis both fit. Characterise the bleeding, ask the red flags, then take the family history.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Deciding she's too young for cancer, or blaming piles.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Open question, then: "What is the blood like, and is it mixed in with the stool?"

grid.label: Opening and rapport
grid.fail: Starts with closed questions about piles.
grid.pass: Introduces, confirms identity, asks an open question and lets her finish.
grid.high: Acknowledges that bowel questions are embarrassing and asks permission before them.

grid.label: Bowel habit and bleeding
grid.fail: Records 'bleeding' without its colour or relation to the stool.
grid.pass: Frequency and consistency now versus before, duration; blood colour, mixed in or on the paper; mucus, urgency, tenesmus.
grid.high: Uses dark blood mixed into the stool to place the source above the anal canal, and quantifies the change from her normal.

grid.label: Red flags (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Omits weight loss or anaemia symptoms.
grid.borderline: Asks about weight loss but not anaemia symptoms or a lump.
grid.pass: Asks about weight loss, abdominal pain, a lump, tiredness or breathlessness, and anal pain or a lump.
grid.high: Quantifies weight loss in kilograms over time, and states the negatives back to her.

grid.label: Colitis and infection
grid.fail: Doesn't consider inflammatory bowel disease or infection.
grid.pass: Asks about night-time symptoms, urgency, mouth ulcers, joint, eye or skin problems, travel, antibiotics and contacts.
grid.high: Explains that nocturnal diarrhoea and extra-intestinal features point to colitis rather than irritable bowel syndrome.

grid.label: Family history, drugs and risk
grid.pass: Family history of bowel cancer or IBD, with ages; anticoagulants, NSAIDs, iron; smoking and alcohol.
grid.high: Asks the age at diagnosis of each affected relative and whether anyone had polyps or womb cancer, for a possible inherited syndrome.

grid.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
grid.fail: Doesn't ask what she is worried about.
grid.pass: Asks what she thinks is going on, what worries her and what she hopes for.
grid.high: Names her fear of cancer honestly and addresses her worry about the colonoscopy.

grid.label: Summary at the signal
grid.fail: Retells the history in order without a working diagnosis.
grid.pass: Concise summary with key positives and negatives, and a differential led by colorectal cancer and colitis.
grid.high: Leads with the positive FIT and red flags, names cancer first, colitis second, and states the family history.

grid.label: Investigation
grid.fail: Reassures her that she's too young, or offers a trial of treatment for irritable bowel.
grid.pass: FIT at least 10 µg Hb/g meets NG12, so she stays on the suspected cancer pathway (28 days); DRE and colonoscopy.
grid.high: Knows a change in bowel habit merits FIT at any adult age; a rectal mass needs no FIT; FIT below 10 doesn't stop referral if concern persists.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Mrs Marsh is 44, with six weeks of looser stools three to four times a day, dark blood mixed in, night-time urgency and 3 kg weight loss. Her FIT is 86. Her father had bowel cancer at 62. The main concern is colorectal cancer; colitis is the main alternative.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Her FIT is above 10, so she meets the NG12 criteria and stays on the suspected cancer pathway, with a diagnosis or exclusion within 28 days. I'd examine her, including a rectal examination, and book a colonoscopy myself.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I'm Dr Shah, one of the surgical trainees. Can I check your name and date of birth? Some of my questions are personal; is it all right to ask them? Tell me what's been happening.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: What were your bowels like before this, and now? Dark blood mixed through the stool usually comes from higher up than piles, so I'd like to understand it.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: How much weight, and over what time? So, to check: no lump in your tummy and nothing around the back passage?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: You said you wake at night to go. That can happen with colitis, but it isn't typical of irritable bowel.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: How old was your dad when he was diagnosed? Has anyone had polyps, or womb cancer?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: You mentioned your colleague. Are you worried this is cancer? I'll be honest: we need to rule it out quickly. What worries you about the camera test?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Please stop there and summarise your history.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Mrs Marsh, 44, has a FIT of 86 with six weeks of looser stools, dark blood mixed in, night-time urgency and 3 kg weight loss. Her father had bowel cancer at 62. There are no anal symptoms. Colorectal cancer must be excluded; colitis is the main alternative.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: She meets the NG12 criteria and stays on the suspected cancer pathway: 28 days to diagnosis or exclusion. I'd examine her, including a rectal examination, and book a colonoscopy with biopsies, which answers both cancer and colitis. For her GP: a change in bowel habit merits FIT at any adult age, a rectal mass needs no FIT, and a FIT below 10 shouldn't stop referral if concern persists.

failures.move: Not asking about weight loss or anaemia symptoms.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: misses the features that raise concern for cancer.

failures.move: Assuming blood is from piles without asking its colour or relation to the stool.
failures.consequence: Dark blood mixed in points above the anal canal; the source is missed.
Misses a first-degree relative with bowel cancer, and any pattern suggesting an inherited syndrome.

failures.move: Reassuring her because of her age.
failures.consequence: A FIT at or above 10 means referral on the suspected cancer pathway whatever her age.

recovery.line: Before we finish, has anyone in your family had bowel cancer, polyps or colitis?
It's one of the things we need to rule out, and that's why I'm arranging the camera test quickly.

knowledge.fact: Offer FIT to adults with a change in bowel habit at any age; under 50, rectal bleeding needs abdominal pain or weight loss as well (1.3.1).
FIT at least 10 µg Hb/g: suspected cancer pathway (1.3.2). Rectal mass, anal mass or anal ulceration: no FIT needed (1.3.1, 1.3.5–1.3.6).
FIT below 10 with strong clinical concern: don't delay referral (1.3.3).
Persistent anorectal bleeding alone with FIT below 10: flexible sigmoidoscopy. CT colonography is equivalent to colonoscopy for detecting cancer.

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Station format: 9-minute stations with 1 minute's reading; introduce yourself and confirm identity at every station

sources.name: NICE NG12: Suspected cancer: recognition and referral
sources.supports: Offer FIT to guide referral in adults with an abdominal mass, a change in bowel habit, iron-deficiency anaemia, aged 40+ with unexplained weight loss and abdominal pain, aged under 50 with rectal bleeding and unexplained abdominal pain or weight loss, aged 50+ with unexplained rectal bleeding, abdominal pain or weight loss, or aged 60+ with anaemia; FIT even after a negative screening FIT; no FIT needed before referral for a rectal mass, unexplained anal mass or anal ulceration (1.3.1, 2023); refer on a suspected cancer pathway if FIT at least 10 µg Hb/g (1.3.2); if FIT below 10 or not returned, safety-net and don't delay referral if strong clinical concern (1.3.3); consider referral for a rectal mass (1.3.5) or an unexplained anal mass or ulceration (1.3.6); suspected cancer pathway: diagnosis or exclusion within 28 days (glossary)

sources.name: NICE HTG690 (formerly DG56): Quantitative faecal immunochemical testing to guide colorectal cancer pathway referral in primary care
sources.version: Published 24 August 2023; migrated from DG56 December 2025
sources.supports: FIT using HM-JACKarc or OC-Sensor recommended for the symptom groups later adopted into NG12 1.3.1 (1.1); suspected cancer pathway referral at 10 µg Hb/g or more (1.2); safety-netting below 10 µg Hb/g (1.3)

sources.name: Monahan KJ, Davies MM et al. Faecal immunochemical testing (FIT) in patients with signs or symptoms of suspected colorectal cancer: a joint guideline from ACPGBI and BSG. Gut 2022
sources.supports: FIT used by primary care to prioritise patients with features of colorectal cancer (rec 1); threshold fHb 10 µg Hb/g or more for urgent referral (rec 2); patients not excluded from referral on FIT alone (rec 3); persistent unexplained symptoms with fHb below 10 referred if concern continues (rec 9); persistent or recurrent anorectal bleeding with fHb below 10: flexible sigmoidoscopy (rec 13); FIT may stratify adults under 50 (rec 17); anal or rectal mass or anal ulceration referred urgently without FIT; CT colonography equivalent to colonoscopy for detecting cancer (rec 19)

partner.opening: Please take a focused history from Mrs Marsh. I'll stop you at 6 minutes to summarise.
partner.actorBrief: You are Helen Marsh, 44, a primary school teacher. Opening line: "The GP sent me because of some bleeding. I'm sure it's nothing." Emotional state: brisk and a little embarrassed, anxious underneath. Volunteer only that your bowels have been looser for about six weeks. Release other facts only when asked (see reveals). Hidden concern: a colleague was diagnosed with bowel cancer at 46 last year; say so only if asked what worries you. You are also dreading "the camera test". Expectation: "something to settle my stomach".

reveals.finding: "Three or four times a day, soft or loose. I used to go once a day."

reveals.trigger: Asks what the blood looks like
reveals.finding: "Dark red, mixed in with it. Most days." Some mucus. No blood on the paper alone.

reveals.trigger: Asks about weight, pain or tiredness
reveals.finding: "About 3 kilos in two months without trying." Mild cramping low on the left. A bit more tired. No lumps. No anal pain.

reveals.trigger: Asks about night-time symptoms or urgency
reveals.finding: "I've been getting up once most nights to go, and I have to rush."

reveals.trigger: Asks about mouth, joints, eyes, skin, travel or antibiotics
reveals.finding: No to all. No travel, no antibiotics, no ill contacts.
"My dad had bowel cancer at 62. He's fine now." No one with colitis, polyps or womb cancer.
No regular medicines. Ibuprofen occasionally. Non-smoker. About 6 units a week.
"A teacher at my school got bowel cancer at 46."
Say: "Please stop there and summarise your history."

push.question: What is your differential?
push.expect: Colorectal cancer; inflammatory bowel disease (colitis); less likely infection.

push.question: What would you arrange, and how fast?
push.expect: FIT at least 10: she meets NG12 criteria and stays on the suspected cancer pathway (28 days); DRE and colonoscopy with biopsies.

push.question: Why does night-time urgency matter?
push.expect: Nocturnal symptoms point to organic disease such as colitis, not irritable bowel syndrome.

curveballs.prompt: Her GP asks: "She's 44 with bleeding only and no other symptoms. Should I have done a FIT?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: Under 50, rectal bleeding alone isn't a FIT criterion; it needs unexplained abdominal pain or weight loss. A change in bowel habit merits FIT at any adult age.

curveballs.prompt: Her FIT had been 4 µg Hb/g, but the symptoms continue.
curveballs.safeAnswer: A low FIT doesn't exclude disease: with ongoing symptoms, weight loss and her family history, refer anyway and assess the whole colon; flexible sigmoidoscopy is suggested only for persistent anorectal bleeding alone.

curveballs.prompt: You feel a hard mass on rectal examination.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Suspected rectal cancer; no FIT needed. Stays on the suspected cancer pathway: colonoscopy with biopsy, then staging.

curveballs.prompt: "Do I really need the camera? Can't I just have tablets?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: Tablets won't tell us the cause; the colonoscopy looks for both cancer and colitis. Explain sedation and what to expect.
